kind: coordinator reconciliation, derived from the row's own counters
question: Does the pack-append amplification explain BOTH sql_ns and commit_ns?

sql_ns.verdict: CONSISTENT. 2.03-2.18 GB of whole-body rewriting in 796.5 ms is 2.55-2.74 GB/s, a plausible memory-bandwidth figure for blob construction plus page-cache insertion. The amplification is a sufficient explanation of the SQL term.

commit_ns.verdict: NOT EXPLAINED BY THE AMPLIFICATION. Rewriting a pack row in place re-dirties the SAME pages; SQLite flushes only the pages dirty at COMMIT, so the bytes reaching the file are the pack's final size, not the sum of its rewrites. The amplification inflates sql_ns (memory work) and NOT commit_ns (flush work). Section 13.3 already flagged that the full 7.72x cannot be present; this records the mechanism of why.

net_attribution.sql_term: well explained by the pack-append amplification - structural, in-thread, reachable without a cache, durability, worker-count or format change
net_attribution.commit_term: a byte-proportional pager flush cost at this transaction geometry; NOT explained by the amplification and NOT by any of the four candidates sections 9-12 eliminated

largest_unattributed_term: commit_ns at 34.2% of the accept span - an INCOMPLETE row, not a pass
SUPERSEDED: Superseded in full by section 15.0 and section 18.2 of README.md. The verdict string below, claiming the amplification does NOT explain commit_ns, is RETRACTED: the rewrites are spread across 17,378 separate transactions and each transaction flushes its own ~132 KB of dirty pack pages at its own COMMIT. The 246,460,518 ns gap between profile_commit_ns and the COMMIT statement total is NOT_MEASURED and is NOT attributable to advance_pack_if_moved (1,250 statements cannot carry more than ~0.5% of it).
